categories.size: No published market total. The main rooms: Bonhams London Asian Art Week, 12–19 May 2025, £10.7m across five sales (Chinese-led); Bonhams New York 'Netsuke from American Collections', closed 17 October, US$567,500 for over 150 lots (year not stated on the page); Lempertz Asian Art, Cologne, 12 December 2025, about €1.4m, every lot sold. categories.record: Netsuke: Bonhams states it holds the world record for a netsuke, US$441,375, sold in 2022 (its own release); the lot — a kirin on a cloud from the Joseph and Elena Kurstin collection, Bonhams New York, 16 December 2022 — is described on an Artdaily page reached through an image-path URL, see unconfirmed. walls.n: UK: the Ivory Act 2018 and the pre-1918 'outstanding value' exemption certificate
walls.cite: Ivory Act 2018, in force 6 June 2022; guidance extended on 28 January 2025 to hippopotamus, killer whale, narwhal and sperm whale ivory. Dealing in ivory is banned unless the item holds a standard exemption registration or a pre-1918 exemption certificate for outstandingly high artistic, cultural or historical value. The exemption 'is designed to be narrow': the applicant pays a £250 non-refundable fee, an expert at one of 12 prescribed museums assesses, APHA decides for the Secretary of State, about three months; no sale until the certificate is granted. Inaccurate information: fine up to £250,000 or up to five years' imprisonment. Ivory netsuke sold in London must pass this gate.
src: gov.uk guidance, Ivory: apply for an exemption certificate (updated 15 May 2025)

categories.note: A connoisseur's market of a few hundred serious buyers. Prices are made by named carvers (Masanao of Kyoto, Kaigyokusai, Tametaka), by provenance from published collections, and by condition. Wood and stag-antler pieces now lead because ivory needs an exemption certificate in Britain and faces bans elsewhere; the Kurstin kirin that set the record was a wood piece. The rooms are Bonhams in London and New York, Lempertz and Van Ham in Cologne, and the London dealers Sydney L. Moss and Max Rutherston, who publish catalogues and sell at TEFAF and the Treasure House Fair. American estates supply the stock; buyers are European, American and increasingly Japanese, who repatriate. Ukiyo-e prints and paintings clear in Hong Kong, where Sotheby's set the Utamaro and Hokusai records in 2025.

walls.n: Firearms law: antiques are exempt only within each state's definition; modern sporting guns need a certificate or licence
walls.cite: Stated from memory, not read on a page in this session: the UK Firearms Act 1968 s.58(2) antique exemption as defined by the Antique Firearms Regulations 2021; the US National Firearms Act and the pre-1899 'antique' definition; the EU Firearms Directive. Figures and thresholds kept out. Shotgun certificates are required for Purdey and Holland & Holland guns in Britain; export to the US runs through import licences on the buyer's side.

categories.note: Two markets share one room. Antique arms and armour (pre-1800 swords, harness, wheellocks) are an art market: Peter Finer sells at TEFAF, Hermann Historica and Bonhams run the sales, provenance from princely armouries makes the price. Sporting guns are a working luxury trade: 'best' London side-by-sides by Purdey, Holland & Holland and Boss trade second-hand through Gavin Gardiner's sales and the makers' own used-gun rooms, and the US is the marginal buyer. American collector firearms are the biggest money: Rock Island sells historical Colts and Winchesters to American buyers at prices that now reach US$5m. What moves it: presidential and military provenance, serial-number-one pieces, condition; what blocks it: firearms law at every border.

walls.n: UAE: the falcon passport and CITES permits
walls.cite: Captive-bred falcons must be registered with the Ministry of Climate Change and Environment, which issues closed rings; the CITES-compliant falcon passport (introduced 2002, the UAE says first in the world) carries falcon and owner details, requires a closed leg ring, is valid three years and allows movement without a separate permit. Otherwise MOCCAE CITES certificates: import permits valid one year, export and re-export permits six months, digital with QR verification. Federal Law No. 5 of 2025: import, re-export or introduction from the sea of CITES-listed species without a valid permit — up to 15 years' imprisonment and AED 2 million.
src: MOCCAE presentation, Regulating falconry in the UAE: registration, permits and conservation (CMS Raptors MoU, March 2026)

categories.note: A seasonal, state-sponsored market. Captive-bred gyrfalcons, sakers, peregrines and hybrids from farms in the US, Europe and the Gulf are sold at live auctions inside the hunting fairs — ADIHEX in Abu Dhabi in late summer, the Saudi Falcons Club's two auctions at Malham from August to November — to Gulf falconers before the hunting season. Pure white gyrs are the trophies and the only birds that reach seven figures in dirhams; the bulk trades at tens of thousands. Clubs supply transport, lodging and sale documents to foreign breeders, and the state carries the conservation story. The wall is CITES: every bird crosses a border on a passport or permit, and the UAE's 2025 law sets prison terms for the undocumented.

Buyers bid from 46 countries at RM Sotheby's; sell-through runs 85–96% at the top houses and 65% at Mecum's volume sale. Both leaders are now owned by art houses: Christie's bought Gooding at the close of 2024, Sotheby's holds RM. What moves prices: chassis history, race provenance, originality and one-off status.

Beside the houses sit the Bond Street dealers Graff and Moussaieff, who buy the top stones at auction and in private and re-cut or re-set them. walls.cite: The Commerce and Economic Development Bureau records that 'with the wine duty removed in 2008' Hong Kong became a regional wine trading and distribution hub and a top global wine auction centre; the policy page lists advance consignment clearance into the Mainland, CEPA zero-tariff access for Hong Kong-made wine, anti-counterfeit work by Customs and Excise, and storage and registration schemes. Buyers are younger than in art: half of Sotheby's wine buyers are under 50. Houses now run retail arms beside the auctions.

categories.record: Codex Sassoon, the oldest near-complete Hebrew Bible, US$38.1m with fees, Sotheby's New York, 16 May 2023, estimate US$30–50m — the most valuable manuscript at auction, beating Leonardo's Codex Leicester (US$30.8m, Christie's 1994, bought by Bill Gates). Bought by Alfred H. Moses for American Friends of ANU; now at the ANU Museum of the Jewish People, Tel Aviv. (A first printing of the US Constitution made US$43.2m at Sotheby's in November 2021, a printed document, not a manuscript.)
categories.note: A dealer-led market with the auctions as its price index. London's Peter Harrington and Maggs Bros and the New York trade buy at Christie's and Sotheby's and sell on at fairs (Firsts London, the New York International Antiquarian Book Fair) and from stock; Heritage in Dallas runs the volume end. Prices rest on edition, condition, completeness and association copies; science (Harvey, Newton), early printing, illuminated manuscripts and modern first editions (Harry Potter, Fleming, Tolkien) are the active shelves. Institutions and their donors buy the trophies: the Codex Sassoon went to a museum through a philanthropist, as did the Codex Leicester to a private owner who lends it. Judaica, Islamic manuscripts and maps are their own circuits.

London's Asian Art Week in May and November is the second pole, where Bonhams sold the Christofides Song ceramics for five times estimate and the dealers Eskenazi and Marchant exhibit. Mainland buyers bid in Hong Kong; new bidders at Sotheby's hit a 14-year high in 2025 even as Christie's Asian totals fell. Sell-through at the mainland houses runs about 70%.

walls.n: Iran: US sanctions and the collapse of Persian carpet exports
walls.cite: Al-Monitor, 23 September 2025: Iran's hand-woven carpet exports fell from over US$2bn in the early 1990s and above US$400m in 2017 to US$41.7m in the year to March 2025 (customs figures), more than 95% below the peak; the US, reimposing sanctions in 2018, had bought over 70% of Iranian hand-woven carpets ('we lost the US', Zahra Kamani, head of the National Carpet Centre); exports now go to 55 countries led by Germany, the UAE, Japan and China; at least two million people depend on weaving; a silk carpet retails at US$30,000–40,000 (trader Hamed Nabizadeh).
src: Al-Monitor, 23 September 2025, Iran's carpet industry unravelling under sanctions

categories.note: A thin market with a long memory. Classical Persian, Mughal and Ottoman carpets of the 16th–17th centuries are sold as works of art at Christie's and Sotheby's in London and New York, mostly within the Islamic weeks, and a handful of records (Clark Sickle-Leaf, Béhague, Vanderbilt) stand for decades. Below them the trade is dealer-run: Nazmiyal in New York, Bausback in Mannheim, the Hamburg and London rug dealers, with Istanbul's bazaar and Tehran as sources. The source is drying: Iran's exports fell from over US$2bn in the early 1990s to US$41.7m in the year to March 2025 after the 2018 US sanctions cut off the buyer of 70% of its hand-woven carpets, so Germany, the UAE and Japan now lead. Provenance from Gilded Age collections (Clark, Vanderbilt, Duke) is what makes a seven-figure price; condition and colour do the rest.
